title: What the venue owner adds to our keyword research

content.job: Standalone list email exploring the central exchange and the roles on each side. Preserve the body exactly. No offer or reply request; send metadata remains proposed.
content.body:
Our team had brought the existing keywords and some proposed additions to the conversation. She explained that the shortened name was familiar to local people, as well as some couples coming from outside the area. If couples use a name like that when they talk about the area, some may use it when they search, and a keyword list put together from outside the market can miss a term like that.

The team agreed to look into her suggestion and share any additional terms they found.

It was a small exchange, but it illustrates something we value in an advertising partnership. Our team contributed the recommendations and the commitment to research. The client contributed context about how people talk about her market.

**Your firsthand knowledge of couples deserves a place alongside our advertising expertise.**

When you're already investing in Google Ads, you want the people supporting you to bring considered recommendations. You also have knowledge gained through the conversations you're having with people who might choose your venue.

Those contributions can work together. The person speaking with couples can offer context that's useful to the team researching how to reach them.

We believe a recommendation should give us something meaningful to discuss with you. There should be room for your experience to contribute while we're considering the strategy, with our team taking responsibility for investigating the questions that arise.

That's what this client brought to the review. She explained a familiar way of referring to the region, and our team gave that suggestion a place in the research conversation.
content.ending:
I want a client to be able to share something from a conversation with couples and know what our team will do with it.

Talk soon,
Whitney

You hire specialists for their advertising expertise. You also know how couples talk about your area, because you hear it in your conversations with them. That knowledge deserves room in the keyword research.

slides.job: Establish the prepared recommendations and the invitation.
slides.text:
In a review with a venue client, we walked through the Google keywords already in her account and the additions we were recommending.

Then we invited her questions and concerns about the list, while the recommendations were still open for discussion.

slides.job: Keep the client's contribution and conditional reasoning exactly as approved.
slides.text:
She raised the shortened name people use for the region.

She explained that it was familiar to local people and to some couples coming from outside the area. The suggestion came from her knowledge of how people refer to the place where the venue operates. If couples use that name in conversation, some may use it when they search, and a keyword list put together from outside the market can miss it.

slides.job: Resolve the exchange with the evidenced research commitment.
slides.text:
We said we'd research it and send her any other terms we turned up.

She supplied the local context. We took responsibility for investigating it, next to the recommendations we'd already brought to the review.

slides.job: Connect the story to an owner who already speaks with couples.
slides.text:
If you're already advertising your venue, you hold this kind of knowledge too.

You hear how couples refer to the location, and how familiar a local name is to someone planning from further away. That perspective can feed the work your advertising team is doing.

slides.job: Explain why an observation need not be a finished advertising recommendation.
slides.text:
She didn't need to arrive with a finished recommendation.

She explained the language she knew and why it might be worth a look. That gave the discussion another direction. Weighing what it meant for the keywords was our job.

slides.job: State the partnership belief with a clear division of work.
slides.text:
**We believe your experience should shape the strategy without handing you our specialist research.**

You bring context from your market. We work out what it means for the advertising. In this exchange, each side knew its part.

slides.job: Pay off the promise through the team's specific response.
slides.text:
Our reply told her what would happen next with her idea.

The conversation produced a specific research question for our team, and a commitment to bring any findings back to her. Her suggestion had somewhere to go.

slides.job: Close for both management and guided-launch readers without an explicit ask.
slides.text:
Whether you want a team to manage your ads or to launch your campaigns and guide you while you run them, your knowledge of couples still belongs in the partnership.

In this review, our recommendations and her local knowledge both had a place in what we agreed to explore next.

caption.body:
You already market your venue, and you're the one hearing how couples describe it, where they're coming from and what they call the area. That's experience a good advertising partnership should be able to use, without asking you to become the keyword researcher.

A keyword discussion with a venue client gives a small example. We reviewed the terms already in place and our proposed additions, then invited her perspective. She raised the abbreviation people use for the region and described its familiarity among locals and some couples visiting from elsewhere.

We agreed to investigate and pass along any further terms we found. The client contributed the context; our team committed to the research.

A prepared recommendation gave us something to discuss, and the client's explanation supplied another possibility to examine. Neither had to replace the other.

For an owner who knows the market firsthand, specialist support should give that knowledge a practical role in what gets considered next.

caption.ending: Her suggestion had a defined next step, with our team responsible for looking into it.

content.title: The regional shorthand in a venue's keyword review
content.script:
A venue client gave our team another phrase to investigate for her Google Ads.

Here's what happened. Our team was reviewing the keywords she already had, along with some additional recommendations. And they asked whether she had any questions or concerns about the list.

She brought up the shorthand people use for her area. She explained that local people use it, and some couples from outside the area do, too. If couples use a name like that when they talk about the area, some of them may use it when they search. A keyword list put together from outside the market can miss a term like that.

Our team said they'd look into it and share any other terms they found.

What stands out to me is how she contributed. She brought something she knew about the way people talk about her market into the research conversation.

When you're speaking with couples, you're hearing language that can be useful to the people working on your ads. We bring our advertising expertise, and you bring that firsthand experience.

I think a good partnership should give both a place in the strategy, so your knowledge of couples can help shape what our team explores.

caption.body:
When you're already investing in Google Ads, you want specialists who can bring a considered recommendation to the table. You also have knowledge of your market that comes from speaking directly with the people choosing a wedding venue.

Those contributions can work together. During a keyword review, our team asked a venue client for questions about the existing terms and the additions being proposed. She suggested looking into a familiar abbreviation for her area, explaining that people used it locally and that it was familiar to some couples travelling in, too. If couples use a name like that in conversation, some may use it when they search.

Our team agreed to research the suggestion and share any further terms they found. Her contribution gave the team another question to pursue.

We believe that kind of exchange belongs in an advertising partnership. The research gives the conversation a starting point, while the client's experience can add something worth exploring. For an owner who already knows the market well, expert support should offer a useful place for that knowledge.

caption.ending:
I want clients to be able to bring us an observation without having to turn it into a finished advertising recommendation.

-Whitney

content.title: A venue's Google budget once Meta started
content.script:
Here's how we set one venue client's Google budget once Meta came in. Our team raised the question with her on a recent call.

When our team reviewed her account, her Google campaigns were already running, spending about $60 a day across two campaigns. With Meta being added, our team asked how she felt about that number. She told us she was spending a lot more than she used to and would love to bring it down a little, but she was open to what we recommended.

Our team was wary of scaling back drastically, and I agreed. Dropping all the way to our usual Google minimum would have been a steep fall from where her account was.

She asked whether we split spend evenly. I explained that we usually start close to 50-50 between Meta and Google, then shift toward whichever one the data supports, based on conversions and quality.

So I recommended starting at about $30 a day on Google, on a fresh campaign. That brings her spend down without slashing it, and it gives us a reset to see whether we can get a better cost per result. She said that sounded good.

From there, our team monitors the results, and if Google earns more budget, we'll talk it through with her in our monthly reports.

I love a question like hers, because it deserves a starting point we can explain and a plan to adjust as the data comes in.

caption.body:
When you're already paying for Google Ads and Meta comes into the mix, the combined spend can feel like a lot. You want to know whether you can bring one down without undoing what's working, and you want a reason behind the number.

On a call with a venue client, our team raised that question with her. Her Google account was spending about $60 a day when our team looked at it, and with Meta being added, she said she'd love to bring that down a little while staying open to our recommendation.

Our team didn't want to cut it drastically. Going all the way to our usual Google minimum would have been a big drop for her account. We also tend to start a Google and Meta pairing near an even split, then move budget toward whichever platform the conversions and lead quality favor.

So we recommended about $30 a day on a fresh Google campaign. It's lower than where she was without being slashed, and the reset gives us a chance to see whether the cost per result can come down. She said that sounded good to her.

From here we keep an eye on the numbers, and if Google earns a bigger share, that conversation happens in our monthly reports.
caption.hook: Adding Meta can make your Google budget look like the obvious place to trim.
caption.ending:
If you've been wondering whether your Google spend still makes sense next to Meta, it's a fair question to put to your ads team, and it deserves an answer with reasons attached.

-Whitney

content.premise: After she added Meta, a venue client asked whether she could bring her Google budget down. Our team weighed keeping her current daily spend against dropping to the usual minimum and chose a middle starting point on a fresh campaign. They also proposed a roughly even Google and Meta split until the data shows where to shift.
content.takeaway: If I ask to spend less on Google, I'll get a reasoned starting point and a plan to adjust from the data, not a yes or a no.

brief_copy.title: The Google keywords already in the account
brief_copy.script:
The Google keywords this venue already had gave our team something useful to work with.

Our team noted that ads were already running when they reviewed the account. And the team thought the existing keywords were good.

So the review included those terms, as well as some recommended additions. We went through what was there and brought the extra ideas into the same discussion.

That matters when you've already put work into advertising. You want someone to understand what's in the account before deciding what to recommend.

In this conversation, the starting point was a positive assessment of the existing terms. The additions were presented alongside them.

I like that there's room to recognise useful work and still identify something else worth exploring. Bringing in specialist support can mean building from what you've already established, with a clear explanation of the recommendations being made.

caption.body:
When you've invested time in an account, you want the next recommendation to reflect an understanding of what is already there. That includes recognising useful choices, as well as finding opportunities to develop the campaign.

In this venue's review, our team began by noting the keywords the venue already had in place. The ads were running before this conversation, and the team considered the existing terms good.

The discussion then covered that list together with proposed additions. The recommendations were presented in relation to the current account, giving the client a view of both the established terms and the further possibilities being considered.

That is a useful part of specialist support for a business already advertising. Previous work provides context for the next decision, and a positive assessment can be part of the review rather than something passed over.

We want our recommendations to reflect an understanding of the work already in place, so the client can see how the proposed changes relate to what has come before.

changes.after:
Should a venue cut its Google budget once Meta ads start? A venue client asked us a version of that on a recent call.

When our team reviewed her account, her Google campaigns were already running, spending about $60 a day across two campaigns. With Meta being added, our team asked how she felt about that number. She told us she was spending a lot more than she used to and would love to bring it down a little, but she was open to what we recommended.

Our team was wary of scaling back drastically, and I agreed. Dropping all the way to our usual Google minimum would have been a steep fall from where her account was.

She asked whether we split spend evenly. I explained that we usually start close to 50-50 between Meta and Google, then shift toward whichever one the data supports, based on conversions and quality.

So I recommended starting at about $30 a day on Google, on a fresh campaign. That brings her spend down without slashing it, and it gives us a reset to see whether we can get a better cost per result. She said that sounded good.

From there, our team monitors the results, and if Google earns more budget, we'll talk it through with her in our monthly reports.

I love a question like hers, because it deserves a starting point we can explain and a plan to adjust as the data comes in.

When you're already paying for Google Ads and Meta comes into the mix, the combined spend can feel like a lot. You want to know whether you can bring one down without undoing what's working, and you want a reason behind the number.

A venue client asked us exactly that. Her Google account was spending about $60 a day when our team looked at it, and with Meta being added, she said she'd love to bring that down a little while staying open to our recommendation.

Our team didn't want to cut it drastically. Going all the way to our usual Google minimum would have been a big drop for her account. We also tend to start a Google and Meta pairing near an even split, then move budget toward whichever platform the conversions and lead quality favor.

So we recommended about $30 a day on a fresh Google campaign. It's lower than where she was without being slashed, and the reset gives us a chance to see whether the cost per result can come down. She said that sounded good to her.

From here we keep an eye on the numbers, and if Google earns a bigger share, that conversation happens in our monthly reports.

caption.body:
Couples can search for a place to get married while also expressing a preference for how the wedding is put together. An all-inclusive option gives them something more specific to look for than a venue in a particular area.

During this Google review, our team saw an opportunity to reflect the venue's all-inclusive offering in the proposed searches. The suggestions included language about both venues and wedding packages.

The rationale came from a real part of the business: this was an option the venue offered, and someone intentionally searching for it could be looking for that kind of wedding arrangement.

Our team also discussed search volume, cost and competition. Those considerations accompanied the recommendations, giving the client more than a list of possible phrases to review.

For a venue investing in specialist support, that explanation matters. The proposal should have a connection to the experience couples can choose, with research informing which possibilities are worth bringing into the discussion.

changes.after:
An all-inclusive option changes how couples look for you. Someone searching for an all-inclusive venue or package is telling you how they want their wedding put together, not only where.

In a Google review with a venue client, our team saw her all-inclusive offer as something that really sets her apart. So the proposed keywords leaned into it, with searches for all-inclusive wedding venues and all-inclusive wedding packages, and our team checked those terms against search volume, cost and competition before presenting them for her review.

The offer shaped a second decision, too. For a higher-ticket purchase like a venue, we usually set up negative keywords so the ads don't show for searches with words like cheap, inexpensive or affordable. But in an earlier conversation about her messaging, she had described her all-inclusive option as an affordable choice and a differentiator. So our team marked "affordable" rather than treating it as an automatic exclusion, and raised it as something we might test down the line, not the first thing to launch with. She said she thought it was worth testing.

That's the kind of detail that only comes from knowing the business behind the account.

stronger_with_permission: Showing the actual regional abbreviation would make the central story more concrete, but it identifies the client's market and stays out under P1.
Saying what the research into the shorthand turned up would give the central story a payoff, but no finding, update or result is recorded, so it stays out under P4.
pack_notes: The locked email body and the locked Reel 1 script share the same conditional sentence about couples searching with a local name and a keyword list missing it; both were written at the gate, so they stay, but WIA may want to vary one before posting.

Reel 2 states the client's Google spend (about $60 a day across two campaigns) and the recommended starting point (about $30 a day); confirm the client is comfortable with her budget figures appearing, even anonymised, as part of P1.
Reel 2 refers to WIA's 'usual Google minimum' without its figure; the $500 a month number was left out because WIA's minimums are not confirmed as published.

Reel 2's line that the fresh campaign gives a reset to see whether cost per result can improve is the team's stated reasoning on the call; the Google Ads lead should confirm the wording. Whitney's aside about Google budgets inflating cost per lead was left out entirely.
Reel 3 states WIA usually excludes words like cheap, inexpensive and affordable for a higher-ticket purchase; the Google Ads lead should confirm this description of negative keywords.
Reel 3 refers to an earlier conversation about the client's messaging, where she called the all-inclusive option affordable; confirm the client is comfortable with that being shared.
Reel 2 and Reel 3 draw on the client's budget and offer details beyond the keyword-review exchange named in P1; extend the client's permission to cover them.
The 'affordable' test was a suggestion the client said was worth testing; copy keeps it as a possible later test, not something launched.

change_notes: Email: kept the locked body; rewrote the opening so it no longer repeats Reel 1's locked line about asking whether she had any questions or concerns; led the subject options with the plan's chosen opening and replaced the third so it no longer echoes carousel slide 1.
Reel 1: kept the locked script and caption body; replaced the on-screen hook with the plan's chosen opening and the cover so the two no longer say nearly the same thing.

Reel 2: rewritten from scratch to the plan's premise (the Google budget decision once Meta was added), from the 13:19 to 17:45 turns in reported speech, with Whitney speaking in the first person for her own recommendation; the brief's existing-keywords script was retired.
Reel 2: left out the client's aside about lead strength and Fallon's prediction of good results at a lower budget, and kept the fresh campaign and monitoring as plans.

Reel 3: kept the locked hook and first screen; rewrote screens 2 and 3 to the plan's premise, so the 'affordable' negative-keyword decision now appears as a possible later test; moved volume, cost and competition into the caption, and kept the market and the abbreviation out.

Carousel: kept the locked slide 3; tightened the other slides and reworded slides 1, 2 and 4 to remove phrases shared with the email and Reel 1; strengthened slide 6 around her not needing a finished recommendation; refreshed the caption opening with the reader's situation.
